description: Explain bash scripts line by line, like regex101 for shell scripts.
cmd.selectDisplayMode: Turn Hover and Panel On or Off
config.language.auto: Follow the VS Code display language.
config.hover.followCursor: When the hover is enabled, show it automatically for the part at the cursor whenever the cursor moves to another position.
config.hover.followDelay: Delay in milliseconds before the hover follows the cursor.
config.inline.maxLength: No longer has an effect (the inline summary was removed).
config.examples.placement: Where worked examples (sample input and output) are shown.
config.examples.placement.first: Right under the part they illustrate, before the explanations of its pieces
config.examples.placement.last: Under the part they illustrate, after the explanations of its pieces
config.hover.enabled: Explain the part of the line under the mouse (a word, an option, an operator) in a hover. **Bash Explainer: Explain Bash on Current Line** (`Ctrl+K Ctrl+E`), which explains the whole line, works even when this is off.
config.inline.enabled: No longer has an effect (the inline summary was removed).
config.inline.deprecated: The inline summary was removed: it no longer has an effect. Hover a word for what it is, `Ctrl+K Ctrl+E` explains the whole line, and `#bashExplainer.hints.names#` marks the command names that do not run what they suggest.
config.hints.deadCode: Fade code that never runs: a branch whose condition the script has already decided (`if false; then …`, a test of a variable set to a known value), the side of `&&` or `||` that is skipped, and what follows `break`, `continue`, `return` or `exit`. It is a hint, not a warning: it is not counted as a problem. Not shown for the shell code of other files (a Dockerfile, a workflow).
config.hints.names: Show a hint after a command name that does not run what its name suggests: a function or an alias that hides a builtin or a program (`cd() { … }`), a builtin turned off by `enable -n`, an alias bash does not expand, `sudo cd` (no such program), a name that runs nothing. Hover it for more; click it to open the panel. In VS Code, `#editor.inlayHints.enabled#` turns all inlay hints on or off.
config.highlight.enabled: Colour shell code from the syntax tree and the models the explanations are made from (semantic tokens), over the editor's own colours: a heredoc ends where bash ends it; commands, builtins, aliases, your functions, options, globs and arithmetic each get a colour, as bash reads them at that place; readonly variables get the colour of constants. Also in the shell code of CI YAML, Makefiles, package.json, Markdown, Jenkinsfiles and bats files (not in Python files and Dockerfiles, whose language servers colour them). To turn it off for one kind of file, set it for that language: `"[makefile]": { "bashExplainer.highlight.enabled": false }`. Needs a theme with semantic highlighting (most have it).
semanticTokenTypes.shebang: The shebang, the first line `#!…`: a comment to bash, which the kernel reads when the file is run as a program. Coloured as a comment unless the theme or `editor.semanticTokenColorCustomizations` has a rule for `shebang`.
semanticTokenModifiers.exported: A variable exported to the commands the shell runs.
semanticTokenModifiers.unquoted: A plain word, not quoted, after the command: one that looks like an option but that the command reads as data (`-v` in `grep -e -v`).
config.panel.autoOpen: Open the explanation panel automatically when a bash script is opened. The panel can always be opened with **Bash Explainer: Open Bash Explanation Panel** or the link in the hover.
config.panel.animations: Animate the explanation panel: rows grow from their parent when they are unfolded, and shrink into it when they are folded, in the Meaning and Reading views, and when a step of the Reading view changes. The panel shows no motion either when the system or VS Code asks for reduced motion (`workbench.reduceMotion`).
config.panel.colors: Where the colours of the parts of a line in the explanation panel come from. VS Code only: the web page keeps its own palettes. In a remote window (WSL, SSH, a container), every theme can be followed when the extension is installed on the local side, and only VS Code's default themes when it runs on the remote side.
config.panel.colors.classic: The panel's own six colours, which keep every kind of part apart.
config.panel.colors.theme: The colours the editor's colour theme gives each part. A part the theme leaves uncoloured, or colours with too little contrast (below 4.5:1, or 7:1 in a high contrast theme), keeps the panel's own colour.
config.panel.colors.themeLike: The theme's colours where they keep the parts apart; where the theme gives two kinds of part one colour (or leaves one uncoloured), a new colour that suits the theme, with enough contrast.
config.shell: The shell scripts are written for. Constructs that shell does not support are pointed out (bash: those newer than `#bashExplainer.bashVersion#`).
config.shell.auto: Detect from the shebang (`#!/bin/sh`…), a `# shellcheck shell=` directive or the file name; bash when unknown
config.shell.sh: POSIX sh (points out what fails in dash and busybox ash)
config.bashVersion: The bash release scripts are explained for. Constructs of a later release (bash 5.3's `${ cmd; }`) are explained as that release runs them, and pointed out as problems when this release lacks them.
config.bashVersion.5.2: bash 5.2 (the release the manual citations follow)
config.diagnostics.enabled: Show warnings in the Problems panel: constructs the script's shell does not support (with quick fixes such as `[[ ]]` → `[ ]` where the meaning is kept), and risks in embedded shell code (script injection, Docker `RUN` pipes without `pipefail`, Python strings without `shell=True`).
config.yq.flavor: Which `yq` scripts use: mikefarah/yq v4, kislyuk/yq (the Python jq wrapper) or mikefarah/yq v3. Their syntax differs.
config.yq.flavor.auto: Tell from the command (options, subcommands, functions) and the file (how yq is installed); mikefarah/yq v4 when unknown
config.examples.enabled: Show worked examples (sample input and output). Turn off to see only the explanations.
config.examples.disabled: Kinds of worked examples not to show, e.g. `regex` or `pipeline`.
config.examples.inHover: Show worked examples in the hover too. Turn off to keep the hover short; the panel still shows them.
config.hover.maxDepth: How many levels of the explanation tree the hover shows (`1`: only the top level; `0`: all). The panel always shows all, folded as you like.
config.notes.pitfalls: Point out common mistakes and how to avoid them: `rm -rf $DIR/…` with an empty `DIR`, unquoted variables, `for f in $(ls)`, `read` without `-r`, `local x=$(cmd)`, `sudo cmd > file`. Errors, lines that fail every time (`[` without `]`, `x = 1`), are said either way.
config.notes.basis: Mark a note, or the explanation of a part, that rests on bash's behaviour rather than the Bash manual ("Not in the manual · checked with bash 5.2"), with a command to try it in your terminal and what it prints. The behaviour is checked by running bash in this project's tests; nothing is run when it is shown.
config.notes.idioms: Add notes about well-known idioms (strict mode, `IFS= read -r`, `trap … EXIT`…).
config.diagnostics.ignore: Warnings not to put in the Problems panel, by the code shown there: `dbracket` (`[[ ]]`), `echoE`, `ampRedirect` (`&>`), `array`, `local`, `echoEscape`, `dockerPipefail`, `injection`, `pythonNoShell`, `pythonInjection`, `crlf` (Windows line ends)…. In a file, `# bash-explainer disable=<code>` turns a warning off for the next line, `# bash-explainer disable-file=<code>` for the whole file (`all` for every warning).
config.diagnostics.embedded: Also put warnings found in shell code inside Dockerfiles, Makefiles, CI YAML, package.json, Markdown and Python into the Problems panel.
config.diagnostics.pitfalls: Also put every warning and caveat the explanations give into the Problems panel, with a code each (`rm-empty-variable-root`, `download-run-by-shell`, `declaration-masks-status`…): warnings for those that can do damage that cannot be undone (`rm -rf $DIR/*`, `rm $f`, `curl … | sh`), information for those that go wrong only with some values or go unnoticed (`for f in $(ls)`, `cat $f`, `read` without `-r`, `local x=$(cmd)`). The errors of the explanations, lines that fail every time (`[` without `]`: `bracket-missing-close`; `x = 1`: `assignment-with-spaces`), are problems either way. With `#bashExplainer.notes.pitfalls#` off, the pitfalls are left out here too. The command-line tool's `--check` fails on an error, and on a warning only with `--strict`.
config.embedded.files: Kinds of files whose shell code is explained.
config.customCommands: Describe commands the dictionary does not know (in-house tools…). Example: `{"deploy": {"summary": "Deploy to production", "options": [{"names": ["-n", "--dry-run"], "description": "only show what would happen"}, {"names": ["-e"], "description": "environment", "takesValue": true}], "operands": [{"description": "service name", "repeat": "+"}]}}`. `repeat` is `?`, `*` or `+`; `subcommands` take the same fields.
config.examples.kind.textFilters: sort, uniq, cut, tr, head, tail, seq…
config.examples.kind.glob: globs, brace expansion, case and find -name patterns
config.embedded.files.yaml: CI YAML (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Azure Pipelines…)
